Fais-moi un diorama pixel-art animé de Paris la nuit, pour servir de fond en boucle à une vidéo lofi de 10 heures sur YouTube. Tout dans un seul fichier HTML (canvas + JavaScript, sans librairie).

AMBIANCE ET COULEURS
Joue à fond sur le contraste chaud / froid : une nuit pluvieuse bleu nuit et violette, avec des coins de lumière chaude. La tour Eiffel dorée, les fenêtres éclairées, les réverbères, un café.

LA SCÈNE (de l'arrière vers l'avant)
- Un ciel en dégradé tramé (dithering façon pixel art), une lune avec un halo, et plusieurs couches de nuages qui défilent lentement, éclairées par la lune au-dessus et par la ville en dessous.
- La tour Eiffel au centre, dorée, avec sa structure en treillis, ses 3 plateformes et son antenne. Son phare tourne et balaie le ciel. Elle scintille régulièrement (des points blancs qui clignotent partout), et une lumière rouge clignote tout en haut.
- Au fond, une ligne de toits parisiens avec des fenêtres qui s'allument et s'éteignent, le dôme doré des Invalides et le Sacré-Cœur blanc sur sa colline.
- Un quai avec des platanes et des réverbères.
- La Seine, avec les reflets de la tour et des lampadaires qui ondulent, de longues traînées de lumière dorée, des ronds de pluie sur l'eau, et un bateau-mouche éclairé qui traverse de temps en temps.
- À gauche, au premier plan, un immeuble haussmannien : toit en zinc mouillé, cheminée qui fume et crache des étincelles, un chat dans une lucarne qui bouge la queue, une fenêtre à la bougie qui vacille, une télé qui clignote en bleu, un balcon en fer forgé, un café avec un store rayé rouge et un néon « CAFÉ » qui grésille de temps en temps.
- À droite, un réverbère parisien avec un halo chaud, qui vacille parfois.
- Tout en bas, une balustrade en fer forgé avec des jardinières.

EFFETS
- De la pluie sur 3 profondeurs. Les gouttes deviennent orange quand elles passent dans une lumière, et elles éclaboussent sur les rebords, le store et la balustrade.
- DES BILLETS QUI TOMBENT DU CIEL : des billets de 100 €, 50 € et 20 €, sur plusieurs profondeurs. Ils virevoltent comme des feuilles (ils se balancent, pivotent, se retournent et brillent quand ils font face).
- De la fumée qui dérive avec le vent, des étincelles, des lumières qui vacillent, et 2 éclairs discrets dans les nuages par boucle.

TECHNIQUE (important)
- Le rendu interne est en 480×270, agrandi ×4 sans lissage (plus proche voisin), pour obtenir un 1920×1080 parfaitement net en plein écran.
- La boucle est PARFAITE et dure 4 minutes : chaque animation est une fonction du temps modulo 240 s (fréquences entières, particules déterministes), donc aucun saut au moment où ça reboucle.
- Touche R : enregistre exactement une boucle en 1920×1080, 60 fps, et télécharge le fichier vidéo (mp4 si possible, sinon webm).
- Touche S : capture PNG en 1080p. Touche F ou double-clic : plein écran. Le curseur se cache quand on ne bouge pas la souris.
- Optimise pour tenir 60 fps : sprites pré-rendus, halos en cache, et un canvas avec l'option willReadFrequently.

Do not transform it into generative art, vector animation, abstract motion graphics, collage, watercolor, paper cutout, cyberpunk, neon graphics, particle art, or clean digital illustration. The objective is for the final animation to feel as if it belongs to the exact same animated world as the reference video. ABSOLUTE VISUAL PRIORITY The most important requirement is: EVERY FRAME MUST LOOK PAINTED FRAME-BY-FRAME WITH A ROUGH PHYSICAL BRUSH. The reference does NOT look like clean digital illustration. It looks like moving paint. Every surface must visibly contain brush strokes. The brush strokes must remain visible in: skies walls skin silhouettes floors shadows clouds clothing light flames landscapes Never cover the image with smooth digital gradients. Never create large perfectly flat computer-generated fills. The paint itself is part of the image. THE ACTUAL PAINTERLY LANGUAGE Reproduce the following characteristics extremely closely. BRUSHWORK Use hundreds of short, directional, overlapping brush strokes. The strokes should feel like they were made with: a dry bristle brush opaque paint rough digital gouache / oil-like paint visible pressure imperfect edges The painting is NOT delicate watercolor. The paint is relatively opaque and dense. Individual brush marks are clearly visible. Backgrounds should contain visible waves of short strokes following the form of the environment. For example: A night sky is not a smooth navy rectangle. It is constructed from many overlapping navy, ultramarine and violet strokes. A brown wall is not a flat brown surface. It contains hundreds of curved brown and ochre marks. A human silhouette is not a clean polygon. It consists of rough overlapping brush masses. BRUSH DIRECTION Brush direction is extremely important. Do not scatter texture randomly. The strokes must describe the shape. Sky: mostly broad horizontal or gently curved strokes. Walls: large irregular swirling strokes. Ground: horizontal scraped strokes. Human torso: strokes following shoulders, chest and spine. Arms: strokes following the direction of the limbs. Flames: vertical upward strokes. Light beams: long vertical cream / yellow / orange strokes. This gives the entire animation the sensation of a moving painting. TEMPORAL PAINT INSTABILITY The painting itself must subtly change over time. Do NOT freeze the texture. At approximately 12–15 visual frames per second, slightly alter: silhouette edges brush positions paint density small color patches highlight shapes shadow shapes The movement should feel like each frame has been repainted. This is essential. However: do NOT create ugly random jitter. The forms remain coherent. The PAINT changes. The OBJECT does not randomly teleport. Think: frame-by-frame painted animation. EXACT COLOR WORLD The entire film must stay inside an extremely restrained palette. DARKS deep navy blue almost-black indigo ultramarine dark desaturated violet extremely dark brown MIDTONES muddy earth brown burnt umber muted ochre dusty violet dark teal-blue LIGHT cream ivory warm pale yellow PRIMARY EMISSIVE COLOR amber gold burnt orange yellow-orange hot cream-white The dominant visual opposition is: DEEP BLUE / BROWN DARKNESS versus INCANDESCENT ORANGE-GOLD LIGHT Do not introduce green neon. Do not introduce magenta neon. Do not introduce cyan sci-fi lighting. Do not create a rainbow palette. LIGHT STYLE Light in the reference is powerful but still PAINTED. The light source may contain: cream-white core → pale yellow → golden yellow → orange → brown-orange halo But its boundary must never look like a perfect digital radial gradient. The edge should be broken. Uneven. Brushy. Fragments of paint should escape from the luminous area. Strong light may overexpose parts of a character into cream or yellow. Nearby surfaces may receive rough orange brush highlights. Use glow, but hide the digital perfection of the glow beneath irregular painted layers. THE LIGHT BEAM When using a beam of light, reproduce the exact visual logic of the reference: A thick, almost white-yellow painted center. Orange-yellow irregular edges. Small broken fragments around the contour. Slight temporal deformation. A soft warm halo surrounding it. The beam may bend abruptly rather than behaving like realistic light. It should look like a giant painted stroke of light entering the world. NOT: laser sci-fi energy volumetric 3D beam hologram HUMAN CHARACTERS Human characters must follow the same rendering logic as the reference. There are two important visual families. DARK HUMAN FIGURES Dark people are painted almost entirely in: navy indigo black-blue Their bodies are simplified but recognizably human. Edges are rough. Anatomy is suggested with large brush masses. Do not draw individual fingers unless necessary. Do not create clean facial features. Faces are mostly dark. When eyes are visible: use two tiny bright cream/white glowing dots. The eyes should create a slightly uncanny, poetic presence. Do NOT make giant cartoon eyes. LUMINOUS HUMAN FIGURES Some characters may become almost entirely orange-gold. Their bodies appear made from light and paint. Use: orange body mass yellow highlights cream highlights small luminous imperfections Parts of the body may disappear into light. Small glowing flecks may exist inside or around the silhouette. Again: do not make these flecks into a conventional particle system. They are tiny PAINT MARKS. CHARACTER EDGES Never use crisp anti-aliased vector edges. Edges should look created by repeated brush contact. Produce: tiny protrusions missing paint rough angular sections occasional duplicated edge strokes small warm rim lights Dark characters illuminated by orange light should receive a thin, irregular orange-painted rim. Not a clean outline. CHARACTER ANIMATION The body animation should feel naturally observed. Use believable human weight. Characters should: lean hesitate reach pull collapse turn bend look upward hold tension Do NOT animate characters as simple stick figures. Use a skeletal system internally if needed, but render over it with large deformable painted masses. The rig must remain invisible. The visible result should look hand-painted. For fast actions: allow individual painted frames to stretch. Use rough smear poses. A hand may become a long brush mark for 1–2 frames. An arm may momentarily distort. The animation must prioritize expressive movement over perfect anatomy. BACKGROUNDS Backgrounds must be simple in geometry but extremely rich in painted texture. Typical structures: large dark painted skies horizontal mountain bands brown cavern-like interiors flat theatrical floors dark voids simple walls simple windows large horizons Do not fill backgrounds with tiny realistic details. The reference creates richness using PAINT, not objects. A wall may contain only one brown color family but hundreds of directional brush marks. COMPOSITION Use graphic, readable compositions. Often: one strong horizontal line one central vertical light one clearly readable human silhouette large areas of darkness Do not overpopulate every frame. Allow negative space. The visual hierarchy must remain immediate. CAMERA Use mostly: static compositions slow push-ins slow pull-backs gentle pans small reframing movements Occasionally use one sudden motion for an emotional transition. Avoid constant 3D camera movement. Avoid orbit cameras. Avoid cinematic drone-like movement. The visual power comes from: paint composition light body language not virtual camera tricks. NO COMPUTER-GRAPHICS LOOK ABSOLUTELY FORBIDDEN: perfect vector paths clean SVG appearance perfect Bezier silhouettes perfect circles everywhere smooth Illustrator gradients slick motion-graphics easing everywhere 3D objects glossy reflections PBR materials neon cyberpunk holographic effects lens flare packs generic particle emitters glitter clouds starfield screensavers fractal visuals HUD interfaces corporate animation flat-design illustration paper collage cut-paper characters chalkboard aesthetic watercolor wash aesthetic anime cartoon character design The final result should look like animated PAINT. STORY THEME Human beings often try to hide their emotions. But emotions continue to move through us. The short film follows one dark-blue human figure whose inner emotional light gradually escapes from their body. No text. No narration. No labels such as: FEAR ANGER SADNESS Everything is communicated visually. 00:00–00:05 SOMETHING ARRIVES Deep navy painted night. Large horizontal fields of rough dark-blue brushwork. A tiny human figure stands alone near the bottom center. The character is painted dark indigo. Almost invisible. Only two tiny pale eyes are visible. Hold the composition. Then: from outside the frame, a gigantic cream-yellow-orange painted beam enters diagonally from above. It suddenly bends downward. Exactly like a massive brush stroke changing direction. The person's posture changes from attack to surprise. Cut just before impact. 00:22–00:25 TRYING TO UNDERSTAND Top-down view. Brown painted desk. Several dirty cream sheets. The papers must still be PAINTED, not photorealistic paper textures. On them: rough black handwritten marks small arrows tiny red marks primitive diagrams human-like shapes Central page: a large irregular black circle. Several red arrows point toward the circle. The circle must look painted. Not geometrically perfect. A dark-blue painted hand enters. It touches the black center. The circle transforms into a dark opening. Camera enters the opening. 00:25–00:28 WE ARE NOT ALONE Transition into a deep teal-blue painted void. The orange human is suspended vertically in the center. Around them: many pale blue-white human bodies. All are painted using the same rough brush treatment. No clean outlines. Some curl inward. Some reach. Some fall. Some sit. Some appear exhausted. Some float. Very thin vertical lines extend upward from several figures. The composition feels like human beings suspended inside an enormous emotional space. The orange person reaches toward one white-blue person. A thin hand-painted orange arc connects their hands. A small orange point appears inside the other person's chest. Then another connection. Then another. Warmth begins spreading between people. Not through particles. Through painted lines and glowing marks. 00:28–00:30 EMOTIONS MOVE BETWEEN US Very dark final landscape. Two small orange points exist far apart. Each belongs to a human silhouette. One orange point moves away from the first chest. It travels through darkness as one rough glowing brush mark. It enters the chest of the second person. Both silhouettes now have warm orange rims. The environment remains dark. No triumphant sunrise. No happy ending cliché. Only two humans. Two small lights. Large dark painted space. Hold for approximately one second. Cut to black. EMOTIONAL TONE The film should feel: mysterious human melancholic strange warm slightly unsettling intimate poetic Never sentimental. Never cute. Never epic superhero cinema. P5.JS RENDERING STRATEGY Do NOT solve the visual style by applying one texture overlay to normal vector graphics. The actual primitives themselves must look painted. Create a custom brush renderer. A brush stroke can be constructed from: an irregular center path multiple semi-opaque deposits varying width small edge fragments slight hue variation rough alpha mask Create reusable systems such as: PaintStroke PaintedShape PaintedHuman PaintedGlow PaintedFlame PaintedBackground PaintedLightBeam PAINTED BACKGROUND TECHNIQUE Instead of: background(20, 30, 70); construct the visible field from many strokes. For example conceptually: base dark fill 150–400 large brush marks using neighboring colors: navy dark violet ultramarine near-black blue Their opacity should overlap. Their direction should follow the environment. Do this for every major surface. HUMAN RENDERING TECHNIQUE Internally animate a skeleton. But render each limb as several irregular painted polygons / brush masses. A forearm should not be: line() or a perfect capsule. Build it from rough overlapping shapes. Slightly regenerate its contour on the handmade animation frame. Use the skeleton only as hidden construction. DUAL FRAME RATE Render the browser smoothly at approximately 60 FPS. But update the PAINTED DRAWING state around: 12 FPS or 15 FPS. For example: handPaintFrame = floor(time * 12) Use this state to control: brush contour variation paint marks small silhouette changes flame shape changes highlight irregularities Camera interpolation can remain smooth. This contrast is extremely important. GLOW Use digital blur internally if necessary. But always place irregular painted marks over and around it. A glow alone must never reveal a perfect Photoshop-like halo. Bright areas must contain visible paint structure. IMPORTANT FINAL CHECK Before accepting any scene, ask: “Could this frame plausibly be a frame from the attached reference animation?” If the answer is no: change it. If it looks like p5.js generative art: change it. If it looks like vector motion design: change it. If it looks like particles with bloom: change it. If it looks like watercolor: change it. If it looks like paper collage: change it. If it looks too clean: change it. If the brush strokes are not immediately visible: change it. FINAL TARGET The viewer should primarily perceive: PAINT MOVING. Not code. Not particles. Not vectors. Not shaders. Not procedural graphics. A dark, expressive animated painting made of rough brush strokes, deep blue silhouettes, brown and violet painted environments, uncanny tiny pale eyes, and violent warm orange light. The attached video is the authority for: palette brush density edge roughness character rendering light behavior background rendering contrast composition movement visual rhythm Match that visual language as closely as possible throughout the full 30 seconds.

Here's the initial prompt, you can always tweak it to fit what you want:

Build a looping "infinite zoom" animation, After Effects style: the camera
travels from landscape to landscape by flying through vintage objects.

LOOK: vintage collage realistic photo landscapes + black & white newspaper
cutout objects (halftone, white paper border, soft shadow). Film grain,
vignette, light flicker.

WORLDS (loop): snowy mountains → pocket watch (swinging on its chain) →
sea cliffs → box camera lens → desert dunes → magnifying glass →
misty lake → hand mirror → back to start.
Extras: floating hat, phone, umbrella, gramophone, key; a 1950s man walking
toward the watch; a whale swimming across the cliffs sky.

HOW:
- Generate everything via the Magnific MCP (Seedream 5 Pro landscapes,
  GPT 2.5 transparent cutouts, depth maps, Kling 2.5 animation, Lyria 3
  music). List the generations + credit cost and wait for my OK first.
- Split each landscape into 3 depth layers from its depth map and fill the
  hidden areas. Parallax: layer scale = camera^Z, Z between 0.45 and 1.22.
- Each portal's glass holds the next world; cut seamlessly when it fills
  the frame.
- Constant speed: exponential zoom to a fixed point, each segment's duration
  proportional to log(zoom). Verify the cuts frame by frame.
- Man & whale: generate on pure green (#00B140), animate in place with
  Kling, key out every frame, build a seamless loop (ping-pong if needed).
- Cutouts animate at 15 fps (on twos).
- 20 s loop, 1920×1080, 30 fps. Music: 96 BPM, cut to exactly 8 bars = 20 s.

DELIVER: an interactive artifact (viewer, AE-style timeline, music +
MP4 download) and a rendered MP4 with music under 30 MB.
Show me screenshots before each expensive step.

2102897952587133299.text:
Here is 7 tips on how to make launch videos like this:

1. Try out different tools (i used @HyperFrames_ for this launch, but it's not perfect and has tons of bugs, and this does this promise it will work for you if you use hyperframes). Go try editframe, remotion, and other options, I've realized that there is no single tool that wins each times. I tried remotion first then went to hyperframes and was satisfied with the result.

2. Mix and match models, I used Opus 5.5 mainly but for some of the harder parts in this video I had Fable 5.1 take it's time and work through it. So be ready to burn some usage since you may need to use tons of models + go through lots of iterations.

3.  DO NOT LET THE AGENT CHOOSE WHAT TO PUT. I told specifically about each part of the video by myself. So don't just yolo it and hope for the best. Tell it, "I want the first part to have a chat thread like slack" (real example of what I said).

4. Give the agent access to your codebase and make the project there. This let's the agent find existing components, and reuse them, or change them for the video. This also gives tons of context about your project.

5. Give your agent a component library of animations. I personally use remocn (shoutout @kapish_dima). My agent did have to migrate some components but it helped a lot, and let my agent give good animations.

6. Have a good landing page. This is one of the best references for a launch video your agent can have. It's more important to focus on the landing page and then do the good launch video.

7. Have good branding. This is one of the most important ones because if you don't have good branding your launch video will just flop. You need to have a good logo, good brand colors, and things like that.

我把自己被封号的那段经历，让 Opus 5.5 做成了一条 80 秒的动画片。

片子没有用图像模型或视频模型，每一帧都是 Opus 5.5 写代码画出来的。

我是真没想到 Opus 5.5 会自己检查画面。它每画完一个镜头，就把十几帧拼成一张图自己看，人物太小、剪刀看不清这些毛病，都是它自己挑出来修改的。

我用的是 GitHub 上的 ClaudeAnimationBase。
作者 John Heibel 用 Opus 5.5 做过一整支 MV，再把经验整理成了这：一个带 31 种表情的现成角色、一份 461 行的规则书、一个能自己检查画面的渲染器。

故事都来自我发过的推：大号 13.9K 被封、重新起号、过年在饭桌上偷看调试日志、在大理把电脑留在酒店到处玩。主角是一个头顶长着韭菜的黄色方块。

1920 帧，我在自己的 Mac 上渲染了 22 分钟。

如果你想给自己做一条有剧情的动画（当然有点抽象，需要耐心看），这个仓库基本就是给你的。

仓库地址放在评论区👇
